preamble: The voiced dental/alveolar affricate /dz/ of medieval Ibero-Romance ended up as the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ in Castilian Spanish, Galician and Asturian. The net change bundles deaffrication, devoicing (merger with the reflex of /ts/) and interdentalization; the relative order is debated, with Mackenzie (2022) arguing that interdental /θ/ and /ð/ emerged by the early 1500s and /ð/ then merged into /θ/. Outside western Ibero-Romance the outcome is unusual: elsewhere /dz/ typically deaffricates to /z/ or merges with /ts/.

examples.from: Old Spanish fazer [faˈdzer] 'to do, make' (< Latin facere)
examples.note: Old Spanish intervocalic z spelled /dz/; after deaffrication and devoicing it merged with the reflex of ç /ts/ as Castilian /θ/ (seseo varieties have /s/ instead).
Standard Galician has /θ/ for the old voiced affricate; Portuguese, which kept a voicing contrast, has fazer with /z/, and western Galician seseo areas have /s/.
Asturian shares the Castilian and Galician outcome /θ/ for the medieval sibilant affricates.

sources: Mackenzie, I. (2022). The Genesis of Spanish /θ/: A Revised Model. Languages 7(3), 191. https://doi.org/10.3390/languages7030191
